title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
authors: Ouns El Harzli, Jelle Bor, Linde Wester, Leonid Zhukov, Hanl Park, Jean-François Bobier, Matt Langione, Antonino Marco Saitta, Jonathan Owens, Richard Hart, Yudong Cao, François Jamet
abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive framework to screen new oxygen electrode materials for solid oxide cells by integrating quantum simulation into the materials design workflow. It addresses the challenge of strongly correlated electrons at interfaces by using advanced embedding techniques (GW+DMFT/SEET) that require quantum solvers. The ultimate goal is to bridge fundamental quantum calculations to tangible, large-scale engineering and economic predictions.
main_problem: Predictive design of oxygen electrodes for solid oxide cells (SOFCs/SOECs) is limited by accurately modeling strongly correlated electronic behavior at interfaces.
main_result: The authors propose an end-to-end framework that links industrial performance metrics to quantum simulation requirements for screening new materials.
method: The framework uses a combination of DFT for initial screening, diagrammatic GW-based embedding (GW+DMFT or SEET) to handle correlations, and quantum impurity solvers to calculate necessary Green's functions.
model_or_system: The system is the electrode/electrolyte interface in solid oxide cells, modeled using perovskite and fluorite structures. The electronic problem is mapped onto correlated impurity models solvable via quantum simulation.
key_observables: Oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, electronic conductivity, and macroscopic metrics like area-specific resistance (ASR).
important_parameters: Intermediate temperatures, correlated transition-metal d-states, and the scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation resources.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that quantum computers can efficiently solve the correlated impurity problems, overcoming classical computational bottlenecks associated with growing active spaces.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SOFC/SOEC structure, the end-to-end workflow from industrial problem to quantum simulation, and the systematic construction of the electrode/electrolyte interface supercell.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the industrial materials screening problem, mapping it to quantum-amenable impurity models, calculating microscopic observables (vacancy energetics, conductivity), and finally connecting these to macroscopic engineering metrics and economic value.
why_interesting: The detailed mapping of a complex, industrially relevant many-body problem (solid-state electrochemistry) onto a quantum simulation workflow provides a concrete use case for quantum computation in condensed matter theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic of a SOFC running on air and a fuel that contains H2. At the cath- ode, O2 + 4e−→2O2−; the O2−ions cross the solid ceramic electrolyte to the anode, where H2 + O2−→H2O + 2e−. Since the electrolyte blocks electrons, they must flow through the external circuit, generating current; net reaction: 2H2 + O2 →2H2O. Running it in reverse, i.e. applying an external voltage instead of drawing current, the same cell operates as a SOEC, splitting H2O back into H2 and O2.

Figure 2: End-to-end workflow for quantum-enabled screening of strongly correlated oxygen- electrode materials. Candidate electrode/electrolyte interfaces are first constructed and treated with periodic DFT for all candidates (Tier T0). For the shortlist, a GW-based embedding (GW+DMFT or SEET) maps the strongly correlated local degrees of freedom onto Anderson impurity models (Tier T1), which constitute the quantum-computing subproblem. The resulting interacting Green’s functions and self-energies are embedded back into the lattice to calculate mi- croscopic materials observables, including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. Figure 3: Ideal bulk crystal structures used as the starting point for the atomistic models. Left: cubic perovskite ABO3 (Pm¯3m), with A cations at the cube corners, the B cation at the body center, and oxygen atoms at the face centers. Right: cubic fluorite CeO2 (Fm¯3m), with Ce cations forming a face-centered-cubic sublattice and oxygen atoms occupying the tetrahedral sites. The actual LSCF and GDC structures are obtained from these parent lattices by introducing the appropriate cation substitutions and oxygen non-stoichiometry, followed by structural relaxation.

Figure 4: Illustration of the construction of an electrode/electrolyte interface supercell from the parent perovskite and fluorite structures. The example shows a (001)-oriented, AO-terminated per- ovskite interfaced with a Ce-terminated (001) fluorite structure. In an application to LSCF/GDC, the in-plane surface cells are first made commensurate through an appropriate choice of supercell, relative rotation, and small lattice strain. The terminating planes and their lateral registry are then chosen, an initial interface separation is specified, and the complete atomic structure is re- laxed with DFT.
